reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
General Comment
This manuscript presents the rational design of copper single-atom catalysts (Cu SACs) supported on oxygen-vacancy-rich
TiO2. The formation of [Cu–Ov–Ti] motifs enhances d–d orbital coupling, leading to highly efficient conversion of CO2 to
CH4. The authors utilize DFT calculations along with a comprehensive array of in-situ and operando characterizations,
including electrochemical EPR, Raman spectroscopy, XAS, ATR-SEIRAS. These analyses reveal that the oxygen vacancy-
induced orbital engineering improves CO adsorption, accelerates the C-O bond cleavage of *OCH3 intermediates, and
stabilizes the active sites. Consequently, the Cu-Ti1O3 catalyst achieves an impressive CH4 Faradaic efficiency of up to
76%, a record-high turnover frequency of approximately 24,000 h-1, and remarkable stability over 1,200 hours at industrially
relevant current densities.
While the manuscript presents high-quality and impactful results, it requires further clarification and additional data support. I
suggest acceptance after major revision.
Specific Comments
1. The procedure for in-situ FTIR Au layer deposition, along with the deposition amount and method of the catalyst ink, has
not been clearly described. To ensure experimental reproducibility, these aspects should be clarified in more detail.
2. As is well known, Au itself is an active catalyst for CO2 reduction. If Cu single atoms are deposited on an Au layer, the
influence of Au cannot be excluded. Therefore, in-situ FTIR data obtained from the Au layer alone (without the catalyst)
would be valuable as a reference.
3. For Cu-Ti1O3, the COL peak appears to shift to higher wavenumber with increasing cathodic potential, while Cu-O4(Ti)
exhibits a shift to lower frequencies. Because these trends are nearly opposite, a clear explanation for this contrasting
behavior is necessary.
4. The authors have conducted in-situ Raman experiments; however, the data and the associated discussion presented are
not sufficiently detailed. It has been well established in previous studies that Raman measurements within the 200–600 cm-
1 frequency range can effectively monitor Cu site-adsorbed intermediates under varying potentials. It is recommended that
the authors carry out these experiments and expand their discussion to strengthen this particular aspect of their research.
5. The authors did not describe the experimental conditions for the in-situ Raman measurements. To ensure reproducibility,
detailed information such as the grating, laser source, objective, and other instrumental parameters must be included.
6. Cu single-atom sites have been extensively reported in previous studies, especially those involving N-coordinated Cu
single-atom catalysts. These catalysts often demonstrate a variety of product selectivities, such as CO, formate, or C2+
products, which differ from the results presented in the current study. The authors should cite several of these previous works
and provide additional discussion to better highlight their findings.
7. The authors highlight industrial-level operation as a key strength of the developed catalyst. However, in real industrial flue
gas, impurities such as SO2, NO, and O2 are typically present. To demonstrate the industrial relevance of this work, the
authors are encouraged to conduct additional experiments that examine how CH4 selectivity and overall catalyst
performance are affected when these impurities are co-fed with CO2.
8. Although the authors have carried out various in-situ experiments, the manuscript does not provide morphological or
structural analyses of the catalyst after the long-term stability test. To support the durability claims, post-test characterizations
such as SEM, XRD, or related analyses should be included.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This manuscript presents oxygen vacancy (Ov)-involved orbital engineering for synthesizing a Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst with
localized Cu single-atom sites toward CO2 electroreduction to methane. It was found that [Cu–Ov–Ti] motifs induced the
enhancement of the d–d coupling at the Cu sites, leading to electronic localization. This construction boosted d-π* polar
interactions with adsorbed *CO2 and breakage of the C–O bond in *OCH3, which was proved by in-situ experiments and
calculations. In general, this work provides a new insight into regulating Cu single-atom sites for the generation of methane
product from CO2 electroreduction. The work is novel and important to the field. I suggest the authors further improve this
work before it can be accepted. My detailed comments are listed below.
1. It is worth investigating whether the CO2 flow rate can affect methane selectivity or activity. It is suggested to increase the
CO2 flow rates to see whether it is possible to further boost methane production.
2. Zero-gap electrolyzer was employed to evaluate the stability of catalysts in this work. In consideration of the distinct
interface microenvironment between zero-gap electrolyzer and flow cell, the influence of current density on the product
selectivity for zero-gap electrolyzer should be further explored.
3. The structure of Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst after reaction have been observed, which maintained well. In addition to the atomic
aggregation threatening the catalyst stability, the cathodic corrosion is also a big program (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 143, 3245–
3255 (2021)). Is this Ov-involved construction can overcome this problem?
4. To better understand the high selectivity towards methane on l-Cu sites of Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst, the authors will need to
clearly identify the active site on the Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst rather than TiO2 substrate.
5. The authors proposed that Cu–Ti1O3 could adsorb CO2 strongly due to stronger d-π* polar-interaction than Cu–O4(Ti),
which was proved by the DFT calculations only. More experimental data is needed to support this conclusion.
6. Some recently published related paper are suggested to be cited, for example, Nat Commun 16, 7943 (2025);
Electrochem. Energy Rev. 2024, 7, 10; Nat Commun 14, 6849 (2023); Electrochem. Energy Rev. 7, 5 (2024); Nano Energy,
2025, 133, 110457; Nano Energy, 2024, 128, Part A, 109873; Angewandte Chemie, 2025, 64 (15), e202424098; etc.
7. In the Methods section, some experimental details were not given, such as the parameter of Ni form (i.e., thickness and
pore size), IrOx content, and the scan rate of LSV. The method of in-situ Raman should also be described.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
This manuscript presents a comprehensive study on Cu-based single-atom catalysts (SACs) supported on TiO2 with
oxygen-vacancy-induced orbital engineering for efficient CO2-to-CH4 electroreduction. The authors develop a Cu-Ti1O3
catalyst featuring [Cu-Oᵥ-Ti] motifs that enable strong d-d orbital coupling, leading to enhanced CH4 selectivity, high
Faradaic efficiency (76%), and exceptional long-term stability at 600 mA/cm2. The study combines in-situ experiments and
DFT calculations to elucidate the mechanistic origin of the improved methanation performance. Overall, this work presents a
promising CO2 reduction electrocatalyst with impressive performance; however, further experimental validation is required
to substantiate the proposed mechanism and confirm the robustness of the performance claims. After addressing the
following comments, the manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature Communications.
1. While the manuscript highlights “industrial-level methanation”, the discussion of energy efficiency and techno-economic
implications is somewhat limited. The authors should provide a brief analysis comparing the energy efficiency (38.7%) and
operational voltage (−4.05 ± 0.16 V) with existing industrial electrolysis benchmarks. A table summarizing key performance
metrics versus reported industrial-scale CO2RR systems would enhance practical relevance. Moreover, a supplementary
techno-economic analysis (TEA) should be incorporated to assess the feasibility and competitiveness of the proposed
system under industrial operating conditions.
2. The introduction of oxygen vacancy defects has been employed to construct d-d orbital interactions to optimize catalytic
performance in the authors’ work. The authors should clarify the structure-activity relationship between the oxygen vacancy
concentration and the CO2RR activity. Does there exist an optimal oxygen vacancy concentration that can maximize the
catalytic efficiency?
3. The 1230-hour stability test is remarkable. However, since XRD and XPS have limited detection sensitivity for atomically
dispersed Cu species, post-test EXAFS or HAADF-STEM analysis should be provided to confirm that Cu remains atomically
isolated rather than aggregated into clusters.
4. The manuscript presents DRT and impedance analyses but lacks the equivalent circuit model used for fitting. The
inclusion of the circuit diagram and fitting parameters is essential to validate the extracted charge-transfer resistance values
and ensure proper correlation between EIS and CO2RR kinetics.
5. While the XPS results provide valuable information on the oxidation state of Cu, they alone cannot unambiguously
distinguish between Cu0 and Cu+ species due to the overlap of Cu 2p binding energies. It is therefore recommended to
include Cu LMM Auger spectra to determine the Auger parameter, which offers a more reliable identification of the Cu
oxidation state. The combined XPS-Auger approach would help confirm whether the Cu sites in Cu–Ti1O3 are
predominantly Cu+ or partially reduced Cu0 species, thereby strengthening the discussion of interfacial charge redistribution
and d-d orbital coupling.
6. The claim that reversible Ov occupancy occurs via *OCH3 intermediates is compelling but may benefit from additional
control experiments. It is suggested to perform isotope-labeling (e.g., 13CO2) or potential-step experiments to confirm that
the observed signal reversibility directly correlates with catalytic turnover rather than electrochemical reduction–oxidation of
the lattice.
7. The reported TOFCH4 (24930 h-1) is impressive for single-atom catalysts and thus requires clear justification of the active
site quantification method (e.g., based on ICP-MS, XAS fitting, or XPS). Similarly, please elaborate on the ECSA
determination method and its reliability, as the normalization directly affects the comparative analysis of catalytic activity.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_4:
This manuscript reported an oxygen vacancy mediated d-orbital engineering of Cu-based single-atom catalysts (SACs) for
electrochemical CO2-to-CH4 conversion. The developed Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst could intensify d–d coupling at Cu sites and
further facilitates the transformation of *OCH3 intermediate to CH4 by promoting C–O bond cleavage, enabling highly
Faradaic efficiency of 76% under jCH4 of 670 mA cm–2 and an impressive durability over 1,230 h. Despite the mentioned
remarkable achievement, several major experimental aspects are missing and the evidence provided seems not enough.
Therefore, I would like to recommend its publication if the following issues are well solved:
1. The authors stated that ‘electron enrichment at oxygen vacancy (Ov) occurs in titanium oxide (TiO2)’. Why are Ov
particularly highlighted in TiO2, given that Ov formation is also commonly observed and Ov engineering is widely applied in
rare-earth oxides such as CeO2 (e.g., 10.1038/s41467-024-49981-9; 10.1038/s41467-024-46513-3).
2. The authors emphasizes that this catalyst possesses outstanding performance at an industrial level. It is therefore
recommended to include an overall techno-economic analysis to substantiate this claim and provide a more convincing
evaluation of its practical feasibility.
3. Detailed atomic labels should be included in the diagrams (such as Supplementary Figure 1 and Figure 2) to enhance
rigor and help readers more accurately interpret the structure information of the molecular models.
4. This Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst exhibits exceptional stability for the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to CH4. However, as CH4
is a deeply reduced products with 8-electron transfer process, the high local alkali concentrations and severe salt
precipitation usually hinder long-term stability test. Given this context, the main text should include more detailed
explanations and experimental descriptions on how on how these challenges were mitigated, to provide valuable technical
guidance for researchers in the field.
5. The authors should clarify the necessary of iR compensation in this work, since the reported reduction potential (e.g.,
FECH4= 76% at −0.88 V in flow cells) appears significantly lower than values typically reported in the literature.
6. Minor formatting adjustments are recommended. In particular, the orbital symbols in XPS results (such as 2p, 1s) should
be italicized for consistency with standard scientific conventions.
7. The in-situ time-field E-EMR measurements indeed reveal intriguing phenomena regarding the Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst’s
response to the applied potential. However, based on the current data, the observed decrease in Ov and the formation of
*OCH3 species do not unambiguously demonstrate that *OCH occupies the vacancy sites. The authors are encouraged to
further clarify how basis of this assignment and to rule out alternative possibilities such as the adsorption of H2O, CO2, or
*OH species.

### Reviewer 1

General Comment
This manuscript presents the rational design of copper single-atom catalysts (Cu SACs) supported on oxygen-vacancy-rich
TiO2. The formation of [Cu–Ov–Ti] motifs enhances d–d orbital coupling, leading to highly efficient conversion of CO2 to
CH4. The authors utilize DFT calculations along with a comprehensive array of in-situ and operando characterizations,
including electrochemical EPR, Raman spectroscopy, XAS, ATR-SEIRAS. These analyses reveal that the oxygen vacancy-
induced orbital engineering improves CO adsorption, accelerates the C-O bond cleavage of *OCH3 intermediates, and
stabilizes the active sites. Consequently, the Cu-Ti1O3 catalyst achieves an impressive CH4 Faradaic efficiency of up to
76%, a record-high turnover frequency of approximately 24,000 h-1, and remarkable stability over 1,200 hours at industrially
relevant current densities.
While the manuscript presents high-quality and impactful results, it requires further clarification and additional data support. I
suggest acceptance after major revision.
Specific Comments
1. The procedure for in-situ FTIR Au layer deposition, along with the deposition amount and method of the catalyst ink, has
not been clearly described. To ensure experimental reproducibility, these aspects should be clarified in more detail.
2. As is well known, Au itself is an active catalyst for CO2 reduction. If Cu single atoms are deposited on an Au layer, the
influence of Au cannot be excluded. Therefore, in-situ FTIR data obtained from the Au layer alone (without the catalyst)
would be valuable as a reference.
3. For Cu-Ti1O3, the COL peak appears to shift to higher wavenumber with increasing cathodic potential, while Cu-O4(Ti)
exhibits a shift to lower frequencies. Because these trends are nearly opposite, a clear explanation for this contrasting
behavior is necessary.
4. The authors have conducted in-situ Raman experiments; however, the data and the associated discussion presented are
not sufficiently detailed. It has been well established in previous studies that Raman measurements within the 200–600 cm-
1 frequency range can effectively monitor Cu site-adsorbed intermediates under varying potentials. It is recommended that
the authors carry out these experiments and expand their discussion to strengthen this particular aspect of their research.
5. The authors did not describe the experimental conditions for the in-situ Raman measurements. To ensure reproducibility,
detailed information such as the grating, laser source, objective, and other instrumental parameters must be included.
6. Cu single-atom sites have been extensively reported in previous studies, especially those involving N-coordinated Cu
single-atom catalysts. These catalysts often demonstrate a variety of product selectivities, such as CO, formate, or C2+
products, which differ from the results presented in the current study. The authors should cite several of these previous works
and provide additional discussion to better highlight their findings.
7. The authors highlight industrial-level operation as a key strength of the developed catalyst. However, in real industrial flue
gas, impurities such as SO2, NO, and O2 are typically present. To demonstrate the industrial relevance of this work, the
authors are encouraged to conduct additional experiments that examine how CH4 selectivity and overall catalyst
performance are affected when these impurities are co-fed with CO2.
8. Although the authors have carried out various in-situ experiments, the manuscript does not provide morphological or
structural analyses of the catalyst after the long-term stability test. To support the durability claims, post-test characterizations
such as SEM, XRD, or related analyses should be included.

### Reviewer 2

This manuscript presents oxygen vacancy (Ov)-involved orbital engineering for synthesizing a Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst with
localized Cu single-atom sites toward CO2 electroreduction to methane. It was found that [Cu–Ov–Ti] motifs induced the
enhancement of the d–d coupling at the Cu sites, leading to electronic localization. This construction boosted d-π* polar
interactions with adsorbed *CO2 and breakage of the C–O bond in *OCH3, which was proved by in-situ experiments and
calculations. In general, this work provides a new insight into regulating Cu single-atom sites for the generation of methane
product from CO2 electroreduction. The work is novel and important to the field. I suggest the authors further improve this
work before it can be accepted. My detailed comments are listed below.
1. It is worth investigating whether the CO2 flow rate can affect methane selectivity or activity. It is suggested to increase the
CO2 flow rates to see whether it is possible to further boost methane production.
2. Zero-gap electrolyzer was employed to evaluate the stability of catalysts in this work. In consideration of the distinct
interface microenvironment between zero-gap electrolyzer and flow cell, the influence of current density on the product
selectivity for zero-gap electrolyzer should be further explored.
3. The structure of Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst after reaction have been observed, which maintained well. In addition to the atomic
aggregation threatening the catalyst stability, the cathodic corrosion is also a big program (J. Am. Chem. Soc. 143, 3245–
3255 (2021)). Is this Ov-involved construction can overcome this problem?
4. To better understand the high selectivity towards methane on l-Cu sites of Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst, the authors will need to
clearly identify the active site on the Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst rather than TiO2 substrate.
5. The authors proposed that Cu–Ti1O3 could adsorb CO2 strongly due to stronger d-π* polar-interaction than Cu–O4(Ti),
which was proved by the DFT calculations only. More experimental data is needed to support this conclusion.
6. Some recently published related paper are suggested to be cited, for example, Nat Commun 16, 7943 (2025);
Electrochem. Energy Rev. 2024, 7, 10; Nat Commun 14, 6849 (2023); Electrochem. Energy Rev. 7, 5 (2024); Nano Energy,
2025, 133, 110457; Nano Energy, 2024, 128, Part A, 109873; Angewandte Chemie, 2025, 64 (15), e202424098; etc.
7. In the Methods section, some experimental details were not given, such as the parameter of Ni form (i.e., thickness and
pore size), IrOx content, and the scan rate of LSV. The method of in-situ Raman should also be described.

### Reviewer 3

This manuscript presents a comprehensive study on Cu-based single-atom catalysts (SACs) supported on TiO2 with
oxygen-vacancy-induced orbital engineering for efficient CO2-to-CH4 electroreduction. The authors develop a Cu-Ti1O3
catalyst featuring [Cu-Oᵥ-Ti] motifs that enable strong d-d orbital coupling, leading to enhanced CH4 selectivity, high
Faradaic efficiency (76%), and exceptional long-term stability at 600 mA/cm2. The study combines in-situ experiments and
DFT calculations to elucidate the mechanistic origin of the improved methanation performance. Overall, this work presents a
promising CO2 reduction electrocatalyst with impressive performance; however, further experimental validation is required
to substantiate the proposed mechanism and confirm the robustness of the performance claims. After addressing the
following comments, the manuscript can be considered for publication in Nature Communications.
1. While the manuscript highlights “industrial-level methanation”, the discussion of energy efficiency and techno-economic
implications is somewhat limited. The authors should provide a brief analysis comparing the energy efficiency (38.7%) and
operational voltage (−4.05 ± 0.16 V) with existing industrial electrolysis benchmarks. A table summarizing key performance
metrics versus reported industrial-scale CO2RR systems would enhance practical relevance. Moreover, a supplementary
techno-economic analysis (TEA) should be incorporated to assess the feasibility and competitiveness of the proposed
system under industrial operating conditions.
2. The introduction of oxygen vacancy defects has been employed to construct d-d orbital interactions to optimize catalytic
performance in the authors’ work. The authors should clarify the structure-activity relationship between the oxygen vacancy
concentration and the CO2RR activity. Does there exist an optimal oxygen vacancy concentration that can maximize the
catalytic efficiency?
3. The 1230-hour stability test is remarkable. However, since XRD and XPS have limited detection sensitivity for atomically
dispersed Cu species, post-test EXAFS or HAADF-STEM analysis should be provided to confirm that Cu remains atomically
isolated rather than aggregated into clusters.
4. The manuscript presents DRT and impedance analyses but lacks the equivalent circuit model used for fitting. The
inclusion of the circuit diagram and fitting parameters is essential to validate the extracted charge-transfer resistance values
and ensure proper correlation between EIS and CO2RR kinetics.
5. While the XPS results provide valuable information on the oxidation state of Cu, they alone cannot unambiguously
distinguish between Cu0 and Cu+ species due to the overlap of Cu 2p binding energies. It is therefore recommended to
include Cu LMM Auger spectra to determine the Auger parameter, which offers a more reliable identification of the Cu
oxidation state. The combined XPS-Auger approach would help confirm whether the Cu sites in Cu–Ti1O3 are
predominantly Cu+ or partially reduced Cu0 species, thereby strengthening the discussion of interfacial charge redistribution
and d-d orbital coupling.
6. The claim that reversible Ov occupancy occurs via *OCH3 intermediates is compelling but may benefit from additional
control experiments. It is suggested to perform isotope-labeling (e.g., 13CO2) or potential-step experiments to confirm that
the observed signal reversibility directly correlates with catalytic turnover rather than electrochemical reduction–oxidation of
the lattice.
7. The reported TOFCH4 (24930 h-1) is impressive for single-atom catalysts and thus requires clear justification of the active
site quantification method (e.g., based on ICP-MS, XAS fitting, or XPS). Similarly, please elaborate on the ECSA
determination method and its reliability, as the normalization directly affects the comparative analysis of catalytic activity.

### Reviewer 4

This manuscript reported an oxygen vacancy mediated d-orbital engineering of Cu-based single-atom catalysts (SACs) for
electrochemical CO2-to-CH4 conversion. The developed Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst could intensify d–d coupling at Cu sites and
further facilitates the transformation of *OCH3 intermediate to CH4 by promoting C–O bond cleavage, enabling highly
Faradaic efficiency of 76% under jCH4 of 670 mA cm–2 and an impressive durability over 1,230 h. Despite the mentioned
remarkable achievement, several major experimental aspects are missing and the evidence provided seems not enough.
Therefore, I would like to recommend its publication if the following issues are well solved:
1. The authors stated that ‘electron enrichment at oxygen vacancy (Ov) occurs in titanium oxide (TiO2)’. Why are Ov
particularly highlighted in TiO2, given that Ov formation is also commonly observed and Ov engineering is widely applied in
rare-earth oxides such as CeO2 (e.g., 10.1038/s41467-024-49981-9; 10.1038/s41467-024-46513-3).
2. The authors emphasizes that this catalyst possesses outstanding performance at an industrial level. It is therefore
recommended to include an overall techno-economic analysis to substantiate this claim and provide a more convincing
evaluation of its practical feasibility.
3. Detailed atomic labels should be included in the diagrams (such as Supplementary Figure 1 and Figure 2) to enhance
rigor and help readers more accurately interpret the structure information of the molecular models.
4. This Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst exhibits exceptional stability for the electrochemical conversion of CO2 to CH4. However, as CH4
is a deeply reduced products with 8-electron transfer process, the high local alkali concentrations and severe salt
precipitation usually hinder long-term stability test. Given this context, the main text should include more detailed
explanations and experimental descriptions on how on how these challenges were mitigated, to provide valuable technical
guidance for researchers in the field.
5. The authors should clarify the necessary of iR compensation in this work, since the reported reduction potential (e.g.,
FECH4= 76% at −0.88 V in flow cells) appears significantly lower than values typically reported in the literature.

be italicized for consistency with standard scientific conventions.
7. The in-situ time-field E-EMR measurements indeed reveal intriguing phenomena regarding the Cu–Ti1O3 catalyst’s
response to the applied potential. However, based on the current data, the observed decrease in Ov and the formation of
*OCH3 species do not unambiguously demonstrate that *OCH occupies the vacancy sites. The authors are encouraged to
further clarify how basis of this assignment and to rule out alternative possibilities such as the adsorption of H2O, CO2, or
*OH species.
